newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Government, Buba try to smooth over asset rift.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Government, Buba try to smooth over asset rift.

text.p: The leaders of the German government and the Bundesbank on Wednesday strove to smooth over a bitter fight on revaluing the Bundesbank's official reserves, saying that both sides had found common ground.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, speaking before parliament, said he expected the government and Bundesbank to reach a good agreement on Bonn's plans to revalue gold and currency reserves.
In a rare public fight over the last several days, the Bundesbank criticised the plan, saying it was an attack on the central bank's independence which could lead to a weaker euro.

But Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, speaking at a banking meeting in Interlaken, Switzerland on Wednesday, said he had indications that Finance Minister Theo Waigel would not force a transfer of profit this year, as had originally been planned.

Waigel had sought to transfer profits from the asset revaluation in 1997, giving the government a windfall payment that could be used to cut its budetary deficits and help it qualify for European monetary union (EMU).

"I have the impression that we can find a solution. Whether it needs some change of Bundesbank laws must be investigated," Tietmeyer said. "We have had some indications from Waigel that he is not interested in introducing legislation that would force us to do that (transfer profit) in 1997."
Details of an agreement would still have to be worked out with the Bundesbank and then discussed by the bank's council and the Bonn cabinet, Kohl added.
Waigel was heavily criticised for taking on the highly-regarded Bundesbank, facing an opposition motion on Wednesday that he be sacked.
The centre-right coalition easily won the motion, however, mustering 328 votes against 311 opposition ballots after Kohl threw his weight fully behind the struggling minister.

Apart from the opposition parties, even the influential business daily Handelsblatt said Waigel now had to quit after his grab for gold shook the credibility of Bonn's preparations for EMU but failed to reap the much-needed funds this year.
"Waigel did not get one step closer to fulfilling his aim to meet the Maastricht criteria," it wrote. "There is no way around it. The only thing left for Waigel to do is resign."
Now back to foraging for extra funds, Kohl and Waigel both said Bonn would meet the three percent deficit-to-GDP target for Europe's monetary union (EMU).
Waigel suggested further spending cuts and privatisations to raise 19 billion marks ($11 billion) to keep its 1997 budget on target.

"A delay (in EMU) would have an enormous impact on financial markets and the German economy's chances in the export market," Kohl said. "The German government will keep firmly to the timetable and criteria for currency union."

Analysts said the Bundesbank's tough stand and indications that it will force Bonn to significantly alter its plans shows that the central bank will not simply enter monetary union as a lame-duck institution.

"This may look like a compromise, but it's not. The Bundesbank won. Waigel caved in," said John Butler, senior fixed income analyst at WestLB in Duesseldorf. "This demonstrates what the Bundesbank is capable of."
A wide difference of opinion on the need to delay Europe's monetary union (EMU) emerged within the top leadership of Germany's main opposition Social Democratic (SPD) party.

Gerhard Schroeder, a leading Social Democrat potential candidate for chancellor, was quoted in an article as saying he believed it would be better to delay the launch of Europe's planned single currency than to soften the criteria.
"I would see that as less bad than to ignore the criteria and give up the stability orientation," Schroeder said.
Speaking in the "Bild" mass circulation daily newspaper, however, Schroeder's party chief Oskar Lafontaine had come out with exactly the opposite line.
"Despite all the problems, I am in favour of launching the euro in 1999," Lafontaine said.
A Finance Ministry spokeswoman said that Germany would now likely proceed with a revaluation of Bundesbank currency reserves before assesing the worth of the central bank's gold reserves.
